The expensive part of teaching a robot or a self-driving policy is not the policy. It is the environments — and the environments are limited by how expensive it is to render a plausible, controllable, interactive world. NVIDIA's answer this week was to publish the machinery instead of the demo.

On 5 November the Cosmos platform added **four open-weight checkpoints** to the Cosmos 3 family, all post-trained from Cosmos3-Nano with **16B trainable parameters**, released under **OpenMDW1.1**, which permits commercial as well as non-commercial use.

## The Move

The four checkpoints split along two axes — what you control, and what you get back.

- **Transfer-Auto** is a bidirectional model for offline synthetic driving data: **synchronized video across up to 11 camera views including fisheyes**, with **joint RGB–LiDAR generation**, controlled per camera by World Scenario Map inputs for scene structure and traffic motion, with text prompts for appearance.
- **Sim-Auto** is the causally distilled streaming variant, generating successive chunks of synchronized camera and LiDAR **in a few denoising steps**, using rolling generated history for long interactive rollouts.
- **Sim-Transfer** turns a physics simulator's controls into photorealistic RGB, with **depth, segmentation, edges and blur** as spatial controls. The division of labour is explicit: text guides appearance, while physics and ground truth stay with the simulator.
- **Sim-Bimanual** predicts the next observation directly from robot actions, supporting interactive two-arm simulation for **YAM and AgiBot** embodiments, driven by a policy or by human-operated joysticks. Its mixed-action example uses **59 control values padded to 64**, with a schema defining coordinate frames, rotations, gripper calibration and validity masks — and **T transitions require T+1 observations**.

The training recipe is a **four-stage pipeline**: bidirectional adaptation from complete recorded clips, teacher forcing with future targets masked, consistency distillation down to **four denoising steps**, and a final **self-forcing** stage trained on the student's own generated history, because a mispredicted object becomes context for later frames and errors otherwise compound.

## What It Buys

Streaming generation is cheap in the right places. The backbone is a Mixture-of-Transformers with separate text and visual networks, and each latent time step represents **four RGB frames** — Transfer predicts one step per chunk, the optimized Bimanual setup predicts two. Smaller chunks mean new controls affect generation more often.

The framing is deliberately open: weights, post-training recipes, notebooks and agent skills are published, and the post itself flags the open question — **where these models faithfully support policy learning and evaluation, and where they do not**.

## Why It Matters

For robotics research, the meaningful shift is that a two-arm embodiment's visual consequence of an action no longer requires building a photorealistic simulator or collecting real footage. And for driving, **synchronized camera and LiDAR** matters because appearance and geometry have to agree — a video generator that cannot keep the 3D sensing consistent cannot train a policy on it.

The honest caveat is the one NVIDIA states itself: open weights mean anyone can post-train these for their own sensor rig or embodiment, and anyone can find where the simulation breaks.
